title: Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: In the automotive business, we have very strong multi-year contracts, where there is a raw material indexing mechanism, but it comes with a lag.
epigraph.author: Parag Satpute, Managing Director & Group CEO, Greaves Cotton, Q2 FY27 earnings call, 29 October 2026

web_blocks.text: Greaves has several routes to market, and each carries different cash terms. About 48% of group sales in FY26 went through dealers and distributors, down from 55%, and the network shrank from 1,755 to 1,255 dealers and distributors. The ten largest took 26% of dealer sales [6]. The rest went direct to original equipment manufacturers (OEMs, the companies that build the vehicle or machine carrying a Greaves part), to institutions and defence buyers, and to exports. The shrinkage looks deliberate: management exited two-wheeler parts, construction-equipment parts and some battery and digital platform businesses in FY26, and called the retail clean-up complete in Q1 FY27 [26][3].

web_blocks.caption: Channel map by business
rows: Direct, multi-year contracts with raw-material indexation
Sole engine supplier to a French microcar maker; auto revenue +37% in Q2 FY27 [62][1]
Commercial-vehicle, agri, marine and rail OEMs
New orders from CAT (UK), TAFE, Tata Motors’ international arm [3][1]
Claims a top-three aftermarket position in several vehicle classes [6][52]
“3S” dealers (sales, service, spares) plus direct institutional orders
Largest single order ₹35 crore, including long-term maintenance [46][26]
Fire-pump, marine, agri OEMs; armed forces
Five new agri OEMs in H1 FY27; fire-engine exports began Q1 FY27 [1][25]
Dealer throughput 18 to 25 units a month [62][1]
Dealers, plus lender tie-ups up to 95% of vehicle value
web_blocks.takeaway: The core sells to a few dozen institutions and a dealer base on negotiated or list prices, so its working capital is predictable. The EV businesses sell to thousands of households, run a captive lender and depend on a subsidy the buyer never sees as a separate line. The core sells things; GEML and Greaves Finance sell things and also finance them, which is why group cash behaves so differently from group profit later in this chapter [6][1].

web_blocks.text: OEM supply is where qualification bites. A vehicle maker cannot change an engine supplier mid-programme: the part must pass emission and durability tests and is then written into a multi-year contract. The French microcar maker is the clearest proof of lock-in, because Greaves is its sole engine supplier and confirmed that on 29 October 2026 [62]. Excel adds a second linkage by moving from stand-alone cables to assemblies, which embeds it in the customer’s design [3][1]. Customer shares of revenue are not published. The group says it has no single-customer dependency: its five largest unsecured customers owed ₹53.34 crore, or 19% of trade receivables, against 26% a year earlier [6].

Dealer networks work differently, because Greaves sells to someone who resells. Greaves Retail enrols 20,000+ mechanics in its UPAHAR loyalty programme and had signed up about 350 retailers to a digital platform by May 2026 against a target of 3,000 by FY27, then stopped updating the number after pruning [6][26][3]. Genset aftermarket (spares, service, annual maintenance) grew 35% in FY26 against 20% for the segment[6].

Greaves Electric Mobility Limited (GEML) has 418 dealers against 320 a year earlier, and letters of intent for 160 more. Online platforms are about 13% of retails, and one food-service fleet runs more than 20,000 Ampere units [1][62]. Coverage is uneven: number one in Bihar at about 18% share and number two in Tamil Nadu at about 15%, but only about 3% in the North and West against about 7% in the South and East [62]. These shares come from VAHAN, the government’s vehicle-registration database, so they are registrations, not a company claim. Dealer reach in the North and West is the unfinished part of the build.

web_blocks.caption: Verified plant list and disclosed capacity
rows: Light Engine Unit-V, Shendra, and Light Engine Unit-I, Chikalthana (both Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar)
Dual-conveyor line for single-cylinder engines added in FY26 (plant not specified); genset engines also made here [6][26]
Industrial Engine Units at Chikalthana (J-2A) and SIPCOT, Gummidipoondi (Tamil Nadu)
New cable assembly line in FY26 [6][26]
web_blocks.takeaway: The company counts nine manufacturing clusters, five on a standalone basis [1][6]. Engine and genset capacities are not disclosed, so an outsider cannot measure core utilisation. Only the EV plants have numbers, and the e-2W plant runs at about 40% of design, which means fixed cost is spread over far fewer scooters than the building was made for. [6][1]

web_blocks.text: Raw materials are the main supply risk. The finance chief named the buckets: “aluminium, iron, copper, PGM, Platinum Group of Metals”, with steel also cited [62]. Platinum-group metals coat the catalytic converters that meet emission rules. Core raw-material cost rose from 63.9% of sales in H1 FY26 to 67.8% in H1 FY27, and from 65.6% to 70.9% for the group [1]. Pass-through is slow: OEM contracts index with a lag and relief starts in Q4 FY27, while dealer price lists were revised at the end of Q1 FY27 and take four to five months to show [62]. The EV side is exposed differently. Most Reo parts are imported, cells for the in-house pack need an import licence, and a customs order of 27 January 2024 treats 2018–21 scooter-part imports as complete kits, claiming ₹56.44 crore plus interest and penalty, under appeal [36][1][6]. GEML’s answer is a rare-earth-free motor, planned for new e-2W launches in Q4 FY27 [1].

Prices are set in three ways: negotiated for OEMs, circulated list prices for dealers, and published prices for scooters, such as ₹1,29,999 for the Ampere Nexus EX+ [1][6]. The company then gives some back. Discounts and incentives cut contracted revenue of ₹3,511.92 crore by ₹75.30 crore to the reported ₹3,436.62 crore in FY26, after a ₹84.30 crore cut the year before [6]. Warranty is the deferred cost: ₹41.15 crore provided, ₹21.31 crore used, and a closing provision of ₹111.31 crore against ₹91.47 crore [6]. Gensets carry a five-year extended warranty, and current Ampere models a 60-month, 75,000-kilometre battery warranty, a long promise for a business that still loses money on each vehicle at the EBITDA line [46][98].

web_blocks.caption: Working-capital days, group and parent company (the core proxy)
web_blocks.takeaway: Days were calculated from the audited statements [6] and match the aggregator’s 37, 50 and 92 for the group in FY26 [60]. The parent-only column is the nearest disclosed proxy for the core: it holds engines, gensets and Greaves Retail but excludes Excel, GEML and Greaves Finance. Suppliers fund the cycle in both columns, which is normal with 60–180-day payment terms [6]. The gap that matters is cash: the parent alone generated ₹347.57 crore in FY26, the group only ₹32.58 crore. By September 2026 the leak had widened, with inventories at ₹455.19 crore from ₹314.32 crore, receivables at ₹416.65 crore from ₹344.81 crore, and group operating cash flow for H1 FY27 at −₹211.82 crore [2].

web_blocks.caption: FY26 audited consolidated revenue-to-cash bridge, scaled to ₹100 of revenue. Materials cost is materials consumed ₹2,136.87 crore, stock-in-trade ₹141.38 crore and inventory change ₹24.79 crore. Other income is ₹49.99 crore less exceptional items of ₹39.34 crore, so profit before tax matches the reported ₹114.91 crore. Capex is purchases of property, plant and equipment ₹36.54 crore plus intangibles ₹59.13 crore.
web_blocks.takeaway: Of every ₹100 of revenue, ₹67.01 went on materials, ₹10.90 on people and ₹15.13 on other operating costs, leaving ₹6.96 of EBITDA. Depreciation took ₹3.17 and interest ₹0.76. Tax took ₹2.32, more than twice the ₹1.03 of profit that survived, most likely because GEML’s losses earned no tax shield (our inference from a 69% effective rate). Operating cash was only ₹0.95, close to profit even though ₹3.17 of depreciation is a non-cash add-back, so roughly ₹3 per ₹100 was absorbed by working capital and the growing vehicle-loan book. Capex of ₹2.78 turned free cash flow, cash from operations less capex, negative by ₹1.84. [6]

web_blocks.text: Cash leaks in four places. The first is the lender: consolidated operations carried a ₹242.21 crore outflow in “other assets”, mostly the Greaves Finance loan book, against ₹31.88 crore at the parent [6]. Loans are an investment of cash, but accounting files them under operations, so a fast-growing lender looks like an operating business that cannot collect. The second is cash tax of ₹79.27 crore, about a third of group EBITDA [6]. The third is capex of ₹95.67 crore, below depreciation of ₹108.79 crore, so the group is not over-building. The fourth is working capital, driven mostly by GEML: H1 FY27 absorbed ₹140.87 crore of inventory and ₹77.30 crore of receivables, partly offset by ₹98.34 crore of extra supplier credit [2]. Management says the ₹530 crore rights issue covers GEML’s burn and working capital for 12–18 months [62].

web_blocks.caption: Subsidy and clawback: how the money moves and where FAME-II broke
rows: The maker certifies each model, including the Phased Manufacturing Programme (PMP) that requires listed parts to be made in India
A ministry notice of 25 May 2023 alleged GEML had not followed PMP guidelines [8]
The maker passes the demand incentive to the buyer as a lower price
Once eligibility was removed, prices rose ₹10,000–20,000 and volume fell from 1,08,710 to 47,818 units [36]
The maker claims reimbursement from the ministry after registration
The ministry can recover paid subsidy with interest, cancel claims and deregister the maker
GEML refunded ₹139.98 crore on 27 October 2023 and provided ₹337.34 crore: ₹477.32 crore in all [8][6]
GEML undertook on 2 August 2024 not to seek FY20–FY23 claims
₹361.93 crore of receivables written off against the provision in FY25 [6]
₹2,500 per kWh, capped at ₹5,000 per e-2W up to ₹1.5 lakh ex-factory; L5 e-3W closed 26 December 2025
Net receivable only ₹12.76 crore at 31 March 2026 [6][57][75]
web_blocks.takeaway: The buyer sees a lower price, the maker carries a receivable from the government, and the government can later challenge parts sourcing. In FAME-II that cost roughly ₹477 crore, extinguished four years of claims and cut volume 56% in FY24 [8][36]. Today the exposure is smaller by design: the cap is ₹5,000 a vehicle against ₹10,000 in FY25, the receivable is under ₹13 crore, and the ministry has paid ₹1,505.30 crore on 20,56,831 e-2Ws through 22 July 2026, about ₹7,300 each (derived) [75]. The subsidy is no longer the profit driver, but it still sets the price gap to petrol scooters, so a further cut hits volume first and margin second.

web_blocks.caption: GEML e-2W unit economics, Q2 FY27 against a year earlier
rows: Dealers; units per dealer a month
web_blocks.takeaway: The arithmetic reconciles: 37,649 units at ₹93,100 is about ₹350 crore, matching the ₹350 crore of two-wheeler revenue reported [62][1]. The ₹13,700 improvement in EBITDA per unit came from a ₹8,000 higher price plus fixed cost spread over more units. At −₹6,300 a unit, breakeven needs a further ₹6,300 of margin per vehicle or much more volume, which management calls “fairly soon” without a date [62]. The L5 three-wheeler differs: ₹59 crore of Q2 revenue on 2,796 units is about ₹2.1 lakh a unit (derived) [1].

web_blocks.text: Engines are harder to read per unit, because no per-engine or genset price is published; the 250 kVA genset page says to contact a dealer [46]. The evidence is at segment level. Engines & Engineering Products earned a 16.3% result margin on ₹2,554.74 crore of FY26 revenue before central costs, and 14.2% on ₹1,478.05 crore in H1 FY27 against 17.0% a year earlier [2]. Core EBITDA fell from 14.4% in FY26 to 11.5% in Q2 FY27 even as medium-horsepower gensets (160–750 kVA) grew 35% and auto engines 37%, so growth is arriving before margin [1][62]. The unit economics turn on two questions: whether pass-through restores the 13–15% target, and whether GEML’s loss per unit closes before its cash does. The next chapter asks whether rivals allow either.

book_paragraphs: Imagine you are standing beside the engine line at Shendra, the Greaves plant outside Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, as a finished engine is lifted onto a truck. Where does it go? You and I could follow it to a three-wheeler assembly line, to a genset yard in Pune, or to a French factory that makes microcars. Every road ends in a different kind of customer, and every customer pays in a different way. That is the first lesson of this chapter. A company that looks like one business from the outside can be four or five, each with its own cash rhythm.

Start with the customers who sign contracts. A vehicle maker cannot swap an engine supplier on a whim. The engine has to pass emission tests and durability tests, and then it is built into a vehicle that will be sold for years. Greaves told its investors that these contracts are multi-year and carry a raw-material clause, “but it comes with a lag”. That one phrase explains the company’s recent margin squeeze. When aluminium, copper and platinum-group metals rise, the clause protects the engine maker only after a few quarters. Until then, Greaves pays the higher price and waits to be reimbursed.

Now meet the customers who never sign anything with Greaves. A mechanic in a small town buys a spare through a retailer, who buys from a distributor, who buys from Greaves. The company counts more than 7,000 retailers and 20,000 mechanics in that chain, yet it pruned the dealer and distributor count from 1,755 to 1,255 in a year. Why would a growing company shrink its own network? Because a thin, active channel beats a thick, sleepy one, and because management exited whole categories such as two-wheeler parts. The lesson for you is to watch what a company stops selling, not only what it starts.

The electric two-wheeler arm sells in an entirely different way. Think of a showroom in Patna or Chennai, where a buyer chooses a scooter by price, range and the monthly loan instalment. The head of that unit, Vikas Singh, put the key number plainly: “Dealer throughput has improved by almost 40% year-on-year per dealer, from 18 to 25 units per month.” If you and I were running that business, this is the figure we would check every quarter, because it says whether the new dealers are real or decorative. It also exposes a gap. The company still holds only about 3% of registrations in the North and West, against about 7% in the South and East.

Here is a question every manufacturer must answer: where do the parts come from? The finance chief named the family of metals, “aluminium, iron, copper, PGM”, the last being platinum-group metals. For the electric side, add battery cells, magnets and tyres, many of them imported. A customs authority once treated imports of scooter parts as complete kits and sent a bill of ₹56.44 crore plus interest, which the company is contesting. So the engineers built a motor that uses no rare-earth magnets at all. When you read a supply chain, look for the single input that a rival or a government can switch off, and ask what the company has done about it.

Then the money. Greaves does not hand you a price list, but its accounts show the rules. Revenue is booked after discounts, and in FY26 those discounts took ₹75.30 crore off contracted sales of ₹3,511.92 crore. Warranty is booked as a promise, and the group now carries a provision of ₹111.31 crore. A battery warranty of five years or 75,000 kilometres is generous for any vehicle maker. For a company still losing money on each electric scooter, it is a bet that the cells will last longer than the losses do.

How fast does cash come back? On the audited numbers, receivables took about 37 days to collect in FY26, inventory sat for about 50 days, and suppliers were paid after about 92 days. Add the first two and subtract the third and you get a negative cycle, which means suppliers fund the business. That is good news. Yet the group generated only ₹32.58 crore of operating cash on ₹3,436.62 crore of revenue, while the parent alone generated ₹347.57 crore. Where did the other ₹315 crore go? Mostly into loans made by the group’s EV lender and into the working capital of the electric arm. Profit that sits in a loan book is real, but you cannot use it to pay a dividend.

The waterfall in the web edition puts a human scale on it. Of each ₹100 Greaves invoiced in FY26, about ₹67 bought materials, ₹11 paid people and ₹15 covered everything else, leaving about ₹7 of EBITDA. Depreciation, interest and tax then took most of what was left, and about ₹1 reached the bottom line as profit. Operating cash was also about ₹1, and capital spending took another ₹2.78, so free cash flow was negative. Where did the tax come from? The parent earns real profit and pays real tax, while the losses in the electric arm do not appear to shelter it. This is an inference, but the 69% effective tax rate points that way.

Charlie Munger said, “Show me the incentive and I’ll show you the outcome.” The incentive here is a subsidy, and it deserves its own paragraph. The government agrees to pay part of the price of each electric scooter. The maker hands the discount to the buyer at the showroom, then claims the money back. If the ministry later decides that the vehicle’s parts were not made in India as the rules required, it can ask for the money back, with interest, and cancel what it has not yet paid. That is what happened here: ₹139.98 crore refunded in October 2023, ₹337.34 crore of receivables provided for, ₹477.32 crore in all. Unit volume fell from 1,08,710 to 47,818 the next year.

What has changed since? The incentive is now capped at ₹5,000 a vehicle, half of what it was in the first year of the new scheme, and the open receivable is under ₹13 crore. The company no longer lives or dies by the cheque. But the buyer still compares a scooter with a petrol one, and a few thousand rupees decides many of those comparisons. If you follow a company like this, ask not only how much subsidy it receives, but how fast it would lose volume if the cap fell again.

What does one scooter earn? The numbers are young and still negative, but they are moving in the right direction. A year ago each unit brought in ₹85,100 and lost ₹20,000 at the EBITDA line. In the latest quarter each brought in ₹93,100 and lost ₹6,300. The plant runs at about 40% of its design, so as volume rises, each scooter carries less of the factory’s fixed cost. We cannot give you the same figures for an engine or a genset, because the company does not publish them. For those, the signal is the segment margin: 16.3% in FY26, then 14.2% in the first half of FY27, with commodity costs to blame.

So what should you carry out of this chapter? First, the core engine and genset businesses turn cash quickly and are funded by suppliers. Second, the group’s cash is being absorbed by lending and by a young EV business, and the rights issue of ₹530 crore is meant to cover that for 12 to 18 months. Third, pass-through lags decide margins when metals rise, and subsidy rules decide volume in electric vehicles. The next question is whether anyone else in these markets can take the profit away. That is Chapter 4.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Cash is where a business tells the truth. Greaves reported a profit in FY26, yet its group operating cash was thirty-two crore on three thousand four hundred crore of sales. The parent alone made three hundred and forty-seven crore, so the engine business is not the problem. When a company runs a manufacturer, a lender and a subsidised EV start-up under one roof, ask which unit is spending the cash, and whether its customers or its owners will pay for it in the end.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Warren Buffett has written that you only learn who has been swimming naked when the tide goes out. A subsidy is a rising tide. It lifts every maker in the segment, and it hides who can earn a margin without it. Greaves has already seen the tide leave once, in FAME-II, and the capped incentive of today is a smaller tide. The useful question is what each scooter earns when the cap falls to zero.

question: How do Greaves products reach customers, and where does cash get stuck on the way?
